about: What a balance pass is allowed to change about each spell, and what each spell is for. Read data/balance/README.md before editing. This file is authoring metadata: the data builder never reads it, so it does not touch the content hash.

objective.confirm: The seeds a tuning pass confirms a new leader on (ADR 0074): 400 seeds from 2000000, clear of the benchmark seeds and of the 200 above them the hold-out replays on. A round's best candidate is chosen on the benchmark seeds out of every candidate of the round, so its score there is the best of several noisy readings and flatters it; it takes the lead only if it also beats the leader here, where it was not chosen. The objective at 200 seeds moves 2.6 from one seed block to the next on the same content, and a single move measured neutral at 200 seeds read 2.4 worse at 800. This changes which candidate a pass keeps, never the score a candidate gets.

mirror.reads: Both sides play the content equally well, so everything left is the content: how long a match lasts, how often it is drawn or capped, how often a declaration fizzles. Not who wins it -- two identical deterministic agents on a symmetric board buy the same packages in the same rounds, tie on every initiative and hand the tie to the seat, so the seat question is read on variety instead (ADR 0062).

skill.reads: Playing well still beats playing at random. A change that closes this gap has removed the decisions instead of balancing them.

variety.reads: Whether the content offers a choice, which is a different question from whether a greedy bot takes one. Both sides play greedily four decisions in five and draw uniformly the fifth (ADR 0014), so a spell the argmax always passes over still gets cast and can be read. Every target that needs a spell to be cast in order to mean anything is read here rather than on the mirrored run.

exploit.reads: How far a player who only wants to win gets against the way the game is meant to be played. Greedy is the taste this catalogue is balanced for; agent A is a searched set that shares none of it and beats Greedy anyway. Content where the two are far apart is content that punishes playing it the intended way. Agent A is a panel and the reading is its best exploiter (ADR 0052): one agent only ever reads what that agent happens to punish, and the same one-spell move was worth 0.013 to one of these sets and 0.235 to another (journal, 2026-09-17), so the term named a pair rather than a catalogue. Every set is played and the highest win rate decides the evaluation. A set goes stale when the content moves — a tuning pass changes what there is to exploit — so the newest search joins the panel rather than replacing it, and an older set stays because a moved catalogue sometimes blinds the newer ones and not it. kill-first is the one set searched on a catalogue other than this one, the weakened Crushing Stomp of that same entry, and it takes every match on both: a set fitted to a moved catalogue finds another route rather than losing the old one, which is why this term is a constant this file cannot spend content on (journal, 2026-09-17). So what is scored here is no longer whether the best exploiter wins but how fast it does (ADR 0053), and a tie at the top of the panel goes to the fastest win rather than to the first name in the list. On 2026-09-24 the panel was measured again under the stun immunity, the bleed price and the defense ceiling (ADR 0072, 0073, 0076) on the benchmark seeds: search-4, mixture-mean, search-2, search-3 and mixture-worst no longer beat Greedy (0.44 to 0.50), so none of them can be the best exploiter and they left; search-23 and search-21 take every match and joined; kill-first (0.806) left as the weakest of the six that still beat Greedy, so the panel stays at five evaluations a candidate.

objective.score: Sum over the targets of weight * (distance outside the band / scale) ** 2. Zero is on target, lower is better. Metric names are report.json's, so a target and a report row are the same number; spellUsageShare, spellsNeverCast and spellsBarelyCast are the ones the tuner adds, because they need the catalogue and not only the evaluation. A candidate that breaks a constraint is not scored at all. Adding spellsBarelyCast made every score before it incomparable with every score after it: a run reading 40.45 under the old set is not a better run than one reading 41 under this one. ADR 0029 did it again, and harder: seven targets moved off the mirrored run onto the exploring one without their bands changing, which took the core content from 69.39 to 52.00 without a single number in the content moving. ADR 0062 did it a third time: player1WinShare moved from the mirror to the exploring run, which took the shipped content from 285.77 to 42.77 with the content unchanged. ADR 0064 did it a fourth time: tierUsageShare reads the lower Wilson bound of a package's top share against a band of 0.8, not the raw share against the even split every package's floor sits at. ADR 0065 did it a fifth: tierWinSpread reads the lower Newcombe bound of a package's win gap, not the raw gap. ADR 0068 did it a sixth: the mirror's rounds band moved from 8-16 to 10-15 and the exploit floor from 8 to 10, the length the game is designed for. ADR 0071 did it a seventh: that band moved from the mirror to the exploring run. Refreshing the exploit panel on 2026-09-24 did it a sixth time: the evaluation reads other agents. Compare scores only across runs judged by the same set read from the same runs.

targets.why: Equal skill on both sides, so anything away from one half is the content favouring a slot. Read on the exploring run since ADR 0062, for the reason ADR 0029 moved seven targets there: on the greedy mirror under packages both sides buy the same package in the same round, every initiative ties, and the seat breaks the tie -- Player 1 took 400 of 400 on four catalogues in five, so the reading measured the tie-break rule and not the content, and was 243 of an objective of 285.77. On the exploring run the two sides diverge and the question has an answer: 0.44 to 0.495 on the same five catalogues.
A draw is the round cap arriving before either team can finish the other.

The length the game is designed for: ten to fifteen rounds (ADR 0068). Long enough that a bad round can be traded back and the deepest packages, which arrive at round 5 at the earliest since ADR 0066, get played; short enough that the cap of 30 stays out of reach. Read on the exploring run, not the greedy mirror (ADR 0071): two greedy agents play a narrow game that ends sooner than a person's would, and a band on the mirror held every tuning pass at its bottom edge, where any move that shortened the mirror by a tenth of a round was penalised however it played. The mirror read 7.8 at 20 base health under ADR 0066 and 10.05 at 30; the exploring run reads 10.03 at 30.
Matches that run out of rounds mean neither side can convert, usually stacked permanent defense.

Agent A's share of declarations that fizzled. Both agents are the same in a mirrored run, so A is the content's own rate. Mostly targets dying before the action resolves, so it falls on its own as matches lengthen. 21.4% at the last measured run.

Bits over agent A's declared spells. 2.21 at the last measured run over ten distinct spells, of a possible 5.17 over thirty-six. Read on the exploring run (ADR 0029), where it reads 2.530 against 1.992 on a mirrored greedy run: the difference was the argmax passing spells over, not the content failing to offer them.

The largest share of landed casts any one spell takes across the whole catalogue. Since tierUsageShare reads the same thing inside each package and catches what this one hides — a package whose casts all go to one of its spells, small in the total — this stays as the coarse guard and carries half the weight. 0.855 on the core content. Read on the exploring run (ADR 0029), where it reads 0.410 against 0.478 on a mirrored greedy run: the difference was the argmax passing spells over, not the content failing to offer them.

Spells in the catalogue that no declaration ever landed. Needs the catalogue as well as the evaluation, so the tuner computes it. The band is read against what the build carries, not against what is on disk: on the nine-spell core content two spells failing to come up is slack, twelve would be the whole game. Read on the exploring run (ADR 0029), where it reads 0 against 2 on a mirrored greedy run: the difference was the argmax passing spells over, not the content failing to offer them.

Spells taking under 1% of the landed casts of the package that teaches them. The hole spellsNeverCast leaves: pummel took 6 of 5283 landed casts of a mirrored run, which is dead in every sense that decides a game and is not a zero, so a buff that moved it from 4 casts to 6 read as no change at all. Read against the package rather than the catalogue because the package is what one pick buys (ADR 0058): a spell can be rare overall and still be worth the pick that brought it, and a package carrying one spell nobody casts sold that pick short. A spell several packages teach is read against each and counted once. Counts strictly the spells spellsNeverCast does not: a zero is a zero in either reading, and with the same band and weight on both, counting it twice would quietly double what the objective asks of that one case. A run whose content carries no packages reports this as missing rather than as zero. Read on the exploring run (ADR 0029), where it reads 0 against 1 on a mirrored greedy run: the difference was the argmax passing spells over, not the content failing to offer them.

Whether every spell of a package earns part of the pick that bought it (ADR 0058): the share of a package's landed casts its most-cast spell takes, worst package, read as the lower bound of its 95 % Wilson interval (ADR 0064). A package teaching one spell is skipped: it takes all of its own casts whatever the content does. The band is not an even split. Every package that teaches more than one spell teaches two, so 0.5 was the floor of each and the band demanded a perfect split from all eleven at once; a catalogue whose every pair truly splits evenly read 0.667 raw at the median, from sampling alone, and paid 5.6 points no move could remove. Spells sold together must differ in play (ADR 0060), and a heal beside an attack is not cast half the time. What the band refuses is the spell that came along for nothing: 0.8 is the other spell taking at least one cast in five, as far as the sample shows. On the shipped catalogue `tier:soulreaver:v1` reads 0.899 (267 of 286), `tier:deathstalker:v1` 0.861 and `tier:prowler:v1` 0.840. Read on the exploring run (ADR 0029): a greedy argmax monopolises a pair on any numbers.

How many times harder the best attack of a package hits one target than the worst, worst package (ADR 0058). Which spells count is read from the content — is Damage at least a third of what the cast puts on a board, priced with the agents' own weights — never from what its casts landed, so lowering an attack until its hits are all absorbed widens this reading instead of dropping the spell out of it. A spell that is not an attack is not compared: a heal and a control spell with a rider of damage share no unit with one (ADR 0043). Damage is read per target actually hit, which the engine counts, and never per cast: that charged a sweep for its reach rather than for its force. The ratio is floored at half a point and capped at 5. Both readings were cruder until ADR 0043 and between them held this at its cap of 5.000 for every candidate a search could build — 36 of an objective of 42.67, flat, which let tune run 8 nerf `soul_devourer` in exactly this dimension for free. Read on the exploring run (ADR 0029).

The gap between two win shares among the spells of one package, worst package, counting only spells enough sides declared, read as the lower bound of the 95 % Newcombe interval of the difference (ADR 0065). Two spells bought by the same pick should not be worth wildly different results. Read raw it was mostly the size of the samples: a catalogue whose every pair truly wins alike read a worst gap of 0.254 at the median and 0.399 at the 90th percentile on the sides the exploring run gives each package, so the tuner was scoring 1 to 6 points of chance. The bound reads 0 for a gap its sides cannot tell from chance, and a gap they prove close to itself: `tier:blightweaver:v1` wins 0.659 of 22 sides with `tranquilizer_dart` and 0.148 of 27 with `infectious_blast`, 0.511 raw and 0.238 bounded. Read on the exploring run (ADR 0029), where it read 0.148 against 0.322 raw on a mirrored greedy run: the difference was the argmax passing spells over, not the content failing to offer them.
The skill gap. Content that a random agent can hold has stopped asking anything.

Played and reported, not scored (ADR 0053). It is the gate that decides which member of the panel the reading comes from, and it stopped scoring because it is pinned at its ceiling: every catalogue measured reads 1.000 against Greedy once a set is searched against it, three of the five panel members read 1.000 on this one, and the one-spell move that a single agent priced at 116 points of objective is worth nothing at all to a set fitted to the catalogue it faces (journal, 2026-09-17). At weight 2 it was 162.00 of the 172.42 points this content scored, 94 % of an objective it could not move: an offset rather than a target, and the offset ADR 0044 froze content tuning over. Turning the opponent up closes the other end rather than opening this one -- against stun-first the same panel reads 0.175 down to 0.005 -- so there is no room further along this axis either. As a diagnostic it still says something: below 1.000 it names the panel members the content still holds, and its own history is a record of stale agents (0.5875 on d4a21a55, 0.8075 on 938bef5e, 0.9275 on 7e199df4 with search-4) rather than of safe catalogues.

How fast the best exploiter closes it out, which is what the win rate stopped being able to say (ADR 0053). Ten rounds is the floor a match is held to (ADR 0068; it was eight), read on the exploring run since ADR 0071, so this reads: the catalogue should not let a player who only wants to win end it faster than a fair game is expected to last. It reads 5.785 on 7e199df4 for 2.45 of a 12.87 objective, and 7.553 for 0.10 with Crushing Stomp at the weakest of its own bounds, where the win rate reads 1.000 and 162.00 on both, to the decimal. So this is the axis a content move actually travels, and both readings are this panel's, scored the way a tuning pass scores a candidate rather than by fitting a fresh agent to each catalogue. The scale is two rounds, about what one spell's worth of pressure moves it. A clock can be gamed by making every match longer, and what stands against that is the exploring run's own 10-to-15 band and the variety spreads; if a pass starts buying rounds rather than balance, this target needs an upper band too.

noNewStrictDominance.what: A candidate may not add a pair where one spell is strictly better than another: same targeting origin, at least as many targets, cost no higher, critical chance no lower, every effect at least as large, and strictly better on one of them.
noNewStrictDominance.why: A spell three nodes down the tree outclassing a starting spell is what progression means, so the pairs the catalogue already has are not defects to remove. Adding one is: it takes a decision out of a hand that had it. Journal entry ci-9 spent a whole learning investigation discovering the starting kit was shaped that way.

noIndistinguishableSpells.what: No two spells may carry the same cost, critical chance, targeting and effects. The same signature the engine's Spell.Indistinguishable audit compares.
noIndistinguishableSpells.why: The engine plays both, but no result can attribute anything to either, so tuning one moves nothing the other does not.

startingKitOffersAChoice.what: None of the three spells every creature starts with may be strictly better than another. Implied by noNewStrictDominance, named separately because this is the one hand every match is dealt.
startingKitOffersAChoice.why: Journal entry ci-9: heavy_strike was strictly better than basic_attack, and no learner could find a decision that was not there.

spell:wait.name: Wait
spell:wait.intent: The floor of the game: spend the activation on nothing and come back one energy richer. It is what a creature does when everything it knows is too expensive, so it must stay free and it must stay worse than acting.
keep: Free to cast
Never worth more than an attack the creature can already afford

spell:basic_attack.name: Basic Attack
spell:basic_attack.intent: The reliable jab of the starting kit: cheap, certain, no critical. Every other attack in the catalogue is priced against its damage per energy, so moving it moves everything.
keep: The cheapest damaging spell a creature knows on round one
No critical chance: it is the predictable one

spell:heavy_strike.name: Heavy Strike
spell:heavy_strike.intent: The starting kit's commitment: pay more of the round for the bigger opening hit. The decision it exists to pose is spend now or bank for later, so it has to cost what it wins.
keep: Strictly dearer and stronger than Basic Attack, never both cheaper and better
The reason a first round has a choice in it

spell:pummel.name: Pummel
spell:pummel.intent: The Brawler's cheap swing: one energy for a hit that crits two times in three. It buys tempo rather than a big number, and the critical chance is the whole reason to take it over Basic Attack.
keep: At most one energy dearer than Basic Attack
Its critical chance stays its defining stat
spell:pummel.note: check-knobs reports this spell as outclassed, and raising its own bounds is not the way out. At 4 damage it would be strictly better than Lightning Bolt -- same damage, same critical chance, one energy cheaper -- so noNewStrictDominance refuses it, and a wider bound here would only buy candidates the constraints throw away. Measured: its whole box tops out around 5.4 against Lightning Bolt's 6.7, and even a certain critical at 3 damage reaches 6.2. Its other edge, costing 1 against 2, is worth nothing on this rule set: 0 of 319 traced declarations had the caster below 2 energy, so the cost never binds. Making this spell a choice is a move on the pair -- Lightning Bolt down as this one comes up -- which is a two-spell candidate, so neither the sweep nor the paired opening can build it and only the climb can. That is what the search budget is for.

spell:guard.name: Guard
spell:guard.intent: The Brawler's investment: a point of defense on an ally for good, plus a point while the pressure is on. Cheap, repeatable and permanent, which makes it the likeliest single cause of a match no one can finish.
keep: Half of it is permanent and stacks on every cast
Cheaper than any healing spell: it prevents, it does not repair

spell:protective_slam.name: Protective Slam
spell:protective_slam.intent: The Mercenary's opener, and the branch's answer to armour. Legacy gave its caster a point of defense, which the taxonomy cannot express: a spell has one target origin, so hitting an enemy and protecting an ally are two spells. Protection is expressed as tempo instead -- a slammed enemy acts later -- which is the one protective thing that can be said to an enemy. That also gives it teeth a bigger hit would not have: defense absorbs damage and does nothing to a stagger, so this is what a Brawler stacking Guard and Full Plate is answered with.
keep: Protection through tempo, never armour: it always carries an initiative debuff
Reads as a trade, not a nuke
The stagger is the point; the damage only has to be worth the activation
spell:protective_slam.note: Most of its value was damage on purpose, because the initiative weight was 0.5 on reasoning alone (ADR 0018) and a version built mainly on the debuff would have rested on an unmeasured number. That objection is now spent: ADR 0032 swept the weight alone and moved it to 2.1, and the debuff half of this spell is what moved with it -- 1.6% of the mirror's casts to 7.0%, without a number here changing. The shape is worth revisiting deliberately rather than by default: at 2.1 the debuff is no longer the cheap half.

spell:chain_slash.name: Chain Slash
spell:chain_slash.intent: The Mercenary's payoff, and the only cast in the catalogue that hits exactly two: the rung between a single-target spike and a line-wide storm. It is the reason to walk that line to the end, so it stays expensive and stays late.
keep: Hits exactly two: the one rung between a spike and a storm, and the only spell on it
Expensive and late: the end of the Mercenary's line, never something to open with
spell:chain_slash.note: It used to claim to be 'the largest cast in the catalogue', which was true only while the spells that beat it were disabled. It puts 10 damage on the board, 5 over two targets; `crazed_specter` puts 18 and `tornado` 12, both at the same depth, and `hateful_sacrifice` ties it at 10 on one. Its numbers are not the problem and were left alone: at 10.00 a round it already sits inside the 8-to-14 band tier 3 is being aimed at, and two candidates that made it bigger -- damage 6 at a cost of 4, and damage 6 at a critical chance of 0.6 -- both measured worse than what is authored. What was wrong was the sentence.

spell:thundering_seal.name: Thundering Seal
spell:thundering_seal.intent: Guard grown up: three permanent points of defense on an ally and three more for two rounds. The damage it used to send back to the attacker was not carried over (ADR 0012), so what is left is pure stacking mitigation. It is the one place the Mercenary protects with armour rather than with tempo -- `protective_slam` says 'never armour' and means it -- because the taxonomy has no initiative *buff*, so protecting an ally through tempo cannot be said at all.
keep: Stronger and dearer than Guard
The permanent half stacks on every cast
spell:thundering_seal.note: It read 5.20 a round against a tier-3 band of 8 to 14, so it was raised to the top of its own bounds rather than redesigned: 2 permanent and 2 for a round became 3 and 3 for two, at the same price. Measured, that is 16 casts to 94 and `spellsNeverCast` 6 to 1 -- longer matches (5.56 rounds to 6.33) buy more evolution picks, so more of the catalogue comes up at all. It is not the best score available: 3 permanent and 2 for two rounds reads 34.33 against this one's 39.97, and the difference is `spellsBarelyCast`. Taken deliberately, because the tier's problem is its floor and this is the shape closer to the tier-3 median of about 10.5. Its overlap with `revenant_guards` -- the same two effects on three allies -- is left for the Necromancer's turn.

spell:full_plate.name: Full Plate
spell:full_plate.intent: Armour the Warlord is meant to always wear. Nothing implements passives yet, so it is a self-targeted permanent point of defense that can be cast every single round, and permanent plus repeatable is only bounded by what it costs. It costs one energy for that reason: half a round's income per point, so a creature that armours itself is a creature not attacking, which is the trade the spell should be.
keep: Plate, not a shirt: one cast is armour a creature can feel, and it stacks by being cast again
Never free: a permanent effect nobody pays for has no brake but the round cap
Cheap enough to cast in the rounds that decide the match, or it is not armour
spell:full_plate.note: Its price is the whole design and the reason its lower bound is one rather than zero. The spell is `SpellType.Passive` in a model where nothing implements a passive, so it is castable, repeatable and permanent; at zero it was unbounded and read 0.65 against the bolt's 6.47, which is how it went 400 matches without a single cast while being the most dangerous spell in the catalogue. Raising the permanent horizon would not have found that -- every reading prices one cast, and one point of defense is one point at any horizon. When a passive becomes a real always-on modifier, this entry is the first to revisit. It is also the Warlord's opener, so `restorative_gush` and `crushing_stomp` are only ever as reachable as it is. At 2 permanent it was declared by 5 sides of 400 on the mirrored run and both children were cast zero times -- a branch nobody walked, whose numbers could not be measured because nobody arrived to use them. At 3 it is declared by 34 and the two behind it are cast 26 and 55. Raising it was the only way to learn anything about the two spells this pass was about.

spell:restorative_gush.name: Restorative Gush
spell:restorative_gush.intent: The big single-target heal: more health back than most single hits take away. It decides on its own whether a war of attrition is winnable, which is why the average match length moves with it.
keep: Heals more in one cast than anything else
Single target: the team heals belong to the Trickster and the Shaman
spell:restorative_gush.note: Its critical chance became a live number with ADR 0033, and that ADR's follow-up said the knob was added here. It was not -- this entry carried three sentences that were false by the time anyone read them: that the knob existed, that the spell was disabled, and that it carried no chance. The knob is real now. The heal goes to 7 with a chance of 0.5, which is 5.62 a round to 8.40 and inside the 8-to-14 band tier 3 is aimed at; its own bounds could not reach the band on the heal alone, which is why the missing knob mattered rather than being a tidy-up.

spell:crushing_stomp.name: Crushing Stomp
spell:crushing_stomp.intent: The Warlord's hammer and the costliest spell in the game: heavy damage and a round of the target doing nothing. Losing an activation is the harshest thing that can happen to a creature, so the price is the point of the spell.
keep: The most expensive cast in the catalogue
Damage and stun together, or it is just an expensive hit
spell:crushing_stomp.note: Raised inside its own bounds to reach its tier: damage 6 to 7, chance 0.667 to 0.8, and the stun from one round to two, all at the same price of 4. That is 6.50 a round to 9.30. The price did not move because the price is the spell -- it is the most expensive cast in the catalogue and that is the first thing its entry keeps. Two rounds of a creature doing nothing is the harshest thing in the game, and it costs two rounds of income to say it. Its chance then came back down from 0.8 to 0.75, one round after it went up: at 0.8 it tied `enraged_charge`, whose entry keeps 'the highest critical chance in the catalogue' as the thing that makes it a Berserker spell rather than an expensive hit. Nothing this spell keeps mentions its chance, so the tie cost the other class its identity and cost this one nothing -- 9.30 a round to 9.12.

spell:enraged_charge.name: Enraged Charge
spell:enraged_charge.intent: The Berserker's gamble, and the one spell in the catalogue whose whole point is the roll. One heavy swing at the highest critical chance anywhere, bought at a price that keeps it to every other round: rage that lands or does not, rather than a steady beat. It is what the class is offered before it is offered anything reliable.
keep: One swing, not a flurry: the roll is the spell, and two effects only split it
The highest critical chance in the catalogue, or it is just an expensive hit
Expensive enough that it cannot be the every-round attack
spell:enraged_charge.note: It reads big per cast on purpose and must be read per round instead: at three energy against an income of two it comes up every other round, so 12.60 a cast is 8.40 a round against `protective_slam`'s 7.33 at two energy. Read per cast it looks like twice the bolt; read per round it is fifteen percent over the spell beside it, which is what a tier-2 opener should be. Its own history is the warning: at 7.00 a cast it was 4.67 a round and fell from 122 landed casts to 32 the moment something at two energy arrived.

spell:tornado.name: Tornado
spell:tornado.intent: The sweep: against a full team it is among the best damage per energy anywhere. Its cost is the first place to look when matches end too quickly, and that is where it has been looked.
keep: The cheapest *damaging* sweep -- never the cheapest spell that reaches three, which is `infectious_blast` at one
Its efficiency comes from breadth, not from the size of the hit
It hits harder than `meteor` at the same price, or the two are one spell
spell:tornado.note: Its price went 2 to 3, which its own intent nominates: at 15.96 a round against a tier-3 band of 8 to 14 it was the second-largest reading in the catalogue, and matches were ending at 6.4 rounds under a band of 8. At 3 it reads 10.64. The alternative measured -- damage 4 to 3, keeping the price at 2 -- reads 7.01 rounds against this one's 6.55 and is the better number, but it turns the spell into a cheaper `meteor`: the same hit on the same three targets, a tier deeper. A tier-3 spell that copies a tier-2 one is the defect this pass exists to remove, so the better reading lost. The old first keep, 'the cheapest spell that reaches three enemies', had been false since `infectious_blast` was enabled at a cost of one.

spell:psycho_rush.name: Psycho Rush
spell:psycho_rush.intent: The Berserker's all-in: close to half a creature in a single cast, and the caster stands there open for a round afterwards. It throws itself at one target and the recoil is the spell -- swing that hard and you are not covering yourself.
keep: The line's gamble: big, single target, expensive
It costs its caster defense, not health: the Berserker is not hurt by its own swing, it is exposed by it
spell:psycho_rush.note: The Berserker is the class whose point is the roll -- `enraged_charge` carries the highest critical chance in the catalogue and says so in its own first line -- and neither spell behind it gambled at all: both sat at 0.33, below the opener. This one now takes 0.5, the top of its own bounds, with the damage at 10: 7.98 a round to 10.00, inside the tier-3 band. Measured, 6 casts to 53. Its second keep used to read 'priced as if the recoil existed, because one day it will'; that day is ADR 0035, and the recoil is on the spell -- 2 defense off its own caster for a round, which is what legacy wrote and what `casterEffects` was built to carry (ADR 0031). It costs 1.30 of the reading, 10.00 a round to 9.13, and the spell stopped reading as strictly better than `engulfing_flames`: the finding was the missing half, not a bound.

spell:poison_slash.name: Poison Slash
spell:poison_slash.intent: The Scoundrel's signature: a small hit that keeps hurting. It is the cheapest way into bleed and the spell that teaches a player what a lasting effect is.
keep: The bleed is the point, the damage is the garnish
The entry-level bleed: weaker than Mortal Wound on every axis
spell:poison_slash.note: These bounds contain a good answer and it is in the interior, not at a corner -- but the measurements below were taken on the Brawler-buffed catalogue of the studio/content branch, where this spell carries a bleed of 1 per round over 2 rounds and Pummel carries 3 damage. This branch carries 1 over 1, so read them as the shape of the curve and not as this catalogue's numbers. There, at 2 damage: 1 over 2 is 6 landed casts; 2 over 2 is 59, still nothing; 2 over 3 takes 5155 of about 8900 with matches at 11.3 rounds, no draw and nothing at the round cap; 3 over 2 reaches the same usage with 12.5% draws; and the corner, 3 over 3, is worse than the middle at 2600, because it kills so fast that a match is 6.0 rounds and there are half as many casts to take a share of. The middle point takes the top spell's share of landed casts from 0.778 to 0.578. On this branch the same spell is at 3 landed casts, and one same-direction pair of steps from 1 over 1 lands on 2 over 2, which measures 310 casts of about 6150 -- fifty times better and still not the interior point, which is two steps of the duration away. Whether the objective keeps that first pair is its own question.

spell:throwing_star.name: Throwing Star
spell:throwing_star.intent: The Prowler's second verb. Its packagemate `poison_slash` concentrates -- one target, hit now and bleeding after -- and this one spreads: the same activation, the same price, across two enemies. A thrown weapon reaching more than one thing it is thrown at is the one shape an opener can carry that the class does not already have, and it is what makes the pick a decision every round rather than a decision once. It used to be the tempo half of the package instead, on two points of Base initiative bought at unlock; the package pays that now and pays it whole (ADR 0059), which left the spell as a smaller copy of its sibling.
keep: Reach is the point: the day it hits one target it is `heavy_strike` with a class on it
Never more targets than `meteor`, which is what a Wizard climbs two levels for
Priced level with `poison_slash`: the choice is the shape of the damage, never what it costs
spell:throwing_star.note: The pair it belongs to was the worst reading in the catalogue. On content `d367db1c` the package split its casts **1813 to 140** -- 93 % to `poison_slash` -- because the two spells did the same thing and one did more of it: identical damage per energy at 3.0, and `poison_slash` taking 6 off a target per activation against 3. Costing 1 was the only edge this spell had, and it is worth nothing here: of **123,592** recorded states where a creature knew it, **1.0 %** sat below 2 energy and 77 % sat at 6 or more. The activation is the scarce thing, not the energy. So the cost went level with its sibling and the reach became the difference, which is a difference the board decides and not the price list. What it must not become is the catalogue's cheap sweep: `meteor` is 3 energy for three targets at level 2, and this is 2 for two at level 1 -- dearer per target, shorter reach, and that ordering is the reason a Wizard still climbs. If a tuning pass ever makes this the better sweep, the finding is about `meteor`. Measured on the benchmark seeds, the split did not balance, it flipped: this spell went from **7 % to 85 %** of the pair's landed casts on `variety`, and one point less damage or one energy more each sends it back to about 10 %. Against a deterministic greedy a pair's usage is a step in its numbers, and the step sits between two integers, so `criticalChance` is here as the continuous lever to walk it with. Tuning it is still to do.

spell:parasite_jab.name: Parasite Jab
spell:parasite_jab.intent: The Leech's opener and the first spell in the catalogue that feeds its caster (ADR 0031): a modest bite that puts some of what it takes back into whoever threw it. It is deliberately the weaker attack of its tier and the only one that answers being hurt, so the choice it offers is not how hard to hit but whether you need the health.
keep: It always feeds its caster: the bite is the price of the meal, not the point of it
A worse attack than the tier's attacks: the healing is what it is for
Never more healing than a real heal: it is a bite, not a Restorative Gush
spell:parasite_jab.note: The reading that matters is not in the numbers: `ActionScorer.HealScore` counts only the health a target is missing, so at full health this spell is worth its damage alone -- 4.50 against `lightning_bolt`'s 6.47 -- and only passes it once its caster has three points to get back. That is lifesteal's whole feel, and it is emergent rather than authored: a Leech reaches for this when it is hurt and for something else when it is not. `cast_value` cannot see the condition and prices the healing whole, so it reads 6.90 where play reads between 4.50 and 6.90.

spell:hateful_sacrifice.name: Hateful Sacrifice
spell:hateful_sacrifice.intent: The largest single hit in the game, and it costs the caster four health to throw. The sacrifice is the name of the spell and it is finally in it (ADR 0031): the legacy prototype paired a hit of 10 with `SelfDirect Health -4`, and only the first half survived the port.
keep: The heaviest single-target hit
It is paid in the caster's own health: that is the sacrifice the name promises
spell:hateful_sacrifice.note: The self-damage was restored when its tier opened, which `docs/domain/spells.md` said would happen -- 'Psycho Rush and Hateful Sacrifice are still halves of themselves, and are re-authored when their tier is opened'. Its old second keep said the energy price stood in for the missing recoil; the recoil is here, so the stand-in is gone. It reads 10.00 a round to 7.33, just under the tier-3 band of 8 to 14, and that is accepted rather than compensated: `cast_value` charges the four health in full, where a bot pays it only in the rounds where four health is what it had left. Measured, 621 casts to 420.

spell:soul_devourer.name: Soul Devourer
spell:soul_devourer.intent: Parasite Jab grown up: the Leech takes what it hits, and this one takes two things. The health it drinks is the class signature the opener already has; the energy it tears out is this spell's own, the half the port dropped and ADR 0035 gave back.
keep: It takes from what it hits: the Leech's whole line does, and this is the large version
It takes energy, not only health: that is what makes it a Soul Devourer and not a bigger `parasite_jab`
Dearer and heavier than `parasite_jab`, or the opener is the better spell
spell:soul_devourer.note: It was the worst rate in the catalogue at 2.00 a round and cast zero times -- a node on the line rather than a spell, because the half that made it a Soul Devourer was dropped at the port. A caster heal of 5 stood in for that half and got it to 9.00 a round and 343 casts. The drain is now expressible (ADR 0035) and it is back where legacy had it, 2 energy off the target, with the caster heal down from 5 to 4: the heal no longer has to carry a theft it was never about. The drain is worth 0.60 in `cast_value` and that reading is wrong in a way worth saying out loud -- energy is priced at 0.3 a point (ADR 0037, 0.2 before it), and taking two off a creature does not cost it two points of anything, it costs it the cast it was saving for. Nothing in the scorers reads a cast denied, so what this spell is worth will read low here until something does.

spell:momentum.name: Momentum
spell:momentum.intent: The Assassin's free strike: a light hit that costs nothing and gathers energy as it lands. It is Wait with a blade in it -- the same activation and the same price, zero -- and where Wait only gathers, Momentum gathers and cuts. The owner asked for it on 2026-09-25 (journal): an attack that costs no energy, deals two or three and gives two or three back. It used to build energy over the next rounds (`EnergyRegeneration`), and no agent cast it: the top of that box was 2.40 a round against rivals at 7 and more.
keep: Free: it costs no energy, which is the whole point of the spell
An attack on one enemy, and the energy lands on its caster in the same cast
Small on both halves, a hit and an income, never a nuke: the Assassin's filler, not its finisher

spell:death_squad.name: Death Squad
spell:death_squad.intent: The whole squad moves first. One activation buys the team a round of haste, which is what legacy wrote and what ADR 0036 finally made sayable: the Assassin does not out-damage anyone, it gets there first.
keep: Team-wide, or it is one creature's initiative and the Assassin has no reason to own it
One round: haste that lasts is a stat change, not a play
No damage and no energy: it buys tempo and only tempo
spell:death_squad.note: It was **cast 0 times in 400 matches** and its own bounds reached 1.20 a round against a tier-3 band of 8 to 14, so `check-knobs` reported it as a spell no move could make a choice -- correctly, because the numbers were never what was wrong with it. Legacy gave the team +10 initiative and +100% critical for a round; neither was expressible, so it was substituted into the tempo it was meant to *buy*, one energy an ally, and energy was 0.2 a point at the time (0.3 since ADR 0037, which would have read 0.90 -- the same dead spell). As the haste it always was it reads **12.60**. The critical half is still out and is a different shape, not a mirror (ADR 0036). Measured, it goes **0 declarations to 182**, of which 162 land, and applies 288 hastes. But greedy takes it to a **0.333 win share over 36 sides** while the exploring agent reads **0.463 over 54** -- the signature of a spell the scorer overvalues rather than a bad spell, the same shape `infectious_blast` showed from the other side. `mortal_wound` drops 104 declarations to 69 beside it, so the class is being crowded out of its own win condition by its support spell. At an amount of 1 it reads 6.30, below the band, and only 12 sides pick it up -- too few to read, which is why 2 ships. What this really names is the initiative weight: ADR 0032 swept 2.1 on content whose only initiative effect was a *debuff on one enemy*, and this entry asked whether the same price holds for a *buff on three allies*. ADR 0037 re-swept it over eleven points on content that carries this spell, and 2.1 won again -- so the price survives the buff, though it is a narrow minimum rather than a flat step and the question is answered rather than closed. There is no duration knob, because the first keep above says one round and a knob that can spend it is not a bound on the spell, it is a way out of its own identity. The amount stops at 3, whose corner reads **18.90** -- above the band on purpose, so the tuner has somewhere to go, and not a target: initiative is the dearest weight *per point* at 2.1 -- kill at 5.0 and stun at 3.0 are larger numbers, but neither multiplies an authored amount -- which makes this the easiest spell in the catalogue to over-tune.

spell:mortal_wound.name: Mortal Wound
spell:mortal_wound.intent: The bleed that actually kills: a hit now and a heavier wound over the rounds that follow. It is the reason to fear the Assassin and the likeliest single cause of a match that runs away from the loser.
keep: More damage over time than up front
The catalogue's heaviest bleed

spell:noxious_cure.name: Noxious Cure
spell:noxious_cure.intent: The cure is noxious to the cured: the whole team is mended and the whole team is left open for having drunk it. Legacy stripped 2 defense from the allies it healed and ADR 0035 gave that stat back, so the bargain is now written in the currency it was written in. The bargain is the spell: without a cost it is a free team heal, and the Trickster is the class that makes you pay for things.
keep: Team-wide heal: it reaches the team or it is Rejuvenate
It always shreds the allies it heals: the price is paid by the cured, which is what makes it noxious
The shred runs out: a cure that costs the team its armour for good is not a cure
spell:noxious_cure.note: Sized against an initiative weight of 0.5, the bargain broke when ADR 0032 measured that weight at 2.1: a slow of 2 cost 4.2 an ally where the heal of 4 is worth 3.2, the cast read **-3.00 a round** -- worse than doing nothing -- and the price had to come down to a slow of 1 to be payable at all. The cost is now the shred legacy wrote, 2 defense for one round, and it is affordable in a way the substitution never was: defense is 0.65 a point, so the price is 1.30 an ally against a heal worth 3.20. That is the ADR's point in one line -- the spell did not need smaller numbers, it needed the right stat. The bounds stay where they were rebuilt, and the amount reaches 3 because the shred has room the slow did not. Two readings the numbers still hide. `HealScore` counts only the health an ally is missing, so on a whole team this is worth nothing and it is never a free cast. And the debuff is a **cost** although it is written like any other effect -- the targeting origin is what says so, and both `cast_value` and `dominates` had to be taught it: read unsigned, shredding the allies you heal makes this spell read as strictly better than a plain heal of the same size.

spell:tranquilizer_dart.name: Tranquilizer Dart
spell:tranquilizer_dart.intent: The cheap stun: a stolen activation for half what Crushing Stomp asks, and almost nothing else. The Trickster buys the tempo the Warlord pays full price for, and pays for it in damage.
keep: Cheaper than Crushing Stomp and weaker for it
The stun is the spell: the damage is a rounding error, not a second half
spell:tranquilizer_dart.note: It was **1 declaration in 400 matches** -- and legacy is not what went wrong with it. The port is faithful (3 energy, 3 damage, a one-round stun) and so was the relationship it was built on: legacy Crushing Stomp is 4 energy, 6 damage, and a stun of **one round**. The second round is this catalogue's, added in the Warlord pass along with damage 6 to 7 and a critical chance of 0.75, and it turned the cheap stun into a strictly worse expensive one -- 75% of the price for 44% of the reading. Nothing caught it: `outclassed` compares a spell's *ceiling* against a rival's *current* value, and this spell's ceiling sat just under `ice_spear`'s, so the check named the Wizard and never mentioned the Warlord. The fix is this spell's own intent, applied: price **2**, damage 3 to **2**, stun to **2 rounds**. 4.00 a round to 8.00, inside the band and still under `crushing_stomp`'s 9.12 -- cheaper and weaker, which is the first keep, while buying tempo at half the Warlord's price, which is the sentence the intent has always carried. Measured: 1 declaration to **78**, 72 stuns landed, and `crushing_stomp` unmoved at 93.1% over 99. Greedy wins 0.387 of the sides that declare it against the exploring agent's **0.659 over 44** -- greedy under-plays it, which is `death_squad`'s split read the other way round. The `check-knobs` finding stays: its ceiling of 10.00 is held down by a damage bound its own identity requires, and the rival is `ice_spear` at 10.20, so the bounds that need to move are the Wizard's.

spell:infectious_blast.name: Infectious Blast
spell:infectious_blast.intent: The only spell that neither damages nor heals: one energy to strip the armour off the whole enemy team, and it never grows back. It is what the rest of the board hits through, so what it is worth depends on who is casting beside it.
keep: No damage: it is control or it is nothing
The cheapest thing that touches all three enemies
The shred is permanent: the Trickster takes something off the board rather than borrowing it
spell:infectious_blast.note: It carried the substitution ADR 0035 removed, and it carried it at the wrong price: rendered as tempo it read **25.20 a round**, the largest number in the catalogue, and `revenant_guards` and `death_squad` were both reported as having no bounds that could make them a choice beside it. As the defense debuff it always was it reads 11.70, inside the tier-3 band. The `revenant_guards` finding went away without either spell moving; `death_squad` is still reported, now against `revenant_guards` at 15.60, which is its own bounds and not this spell's. The duration knob went with the substitution -- the debuff is permanent, and a permanent duration is not a number the tuner can turn.

spell:lightning_bolt.name: Lightning Bolt
spell:lightning_bolt.intent: The Sorcerer's bread and butter: a modest hit that crits two times in three. It is the caster's mirror of Pummel and the spell every Sorcerer branch gets compared against.
keep: The class's baseline attack: everything deeper in the tree must beat it
spell:lightning_bolt.note: Its price is the open question of this catalogue, so the cost bound is wider than most. At two energy it takes 85% of the landed casts on the core content; at three it takes 36%, matches run 9.5 rounds instead of 8.1, and the objective falls from 104.1 to 19.4. Nothing says three is the end of that curve, so the knob reaches four. Its critical chance was listed here as its identity until a measurement showed the identity does not distinguish it: Pummel carries the same 0.667, and a critical multiplies base damage, so at equal rates it widens the gap it is supposed to close. Against a Pummel at 3 damage, dropping this spell's chance to 0.417 leaves Pummel 448 landed casts of about 5900, 0.317 leaves it 649, and one in six flips the catalogue: Pummel 4986, this spell 754, and eight spells cast instead of seven. The cost is length -- 7.6, 9.2 and 11.3 rounds, with the round-cap share 0.000, 0.045 and 0.100 against a band of 0.05 -- so the objective has a real trade to arbitrate, and none of that range was reachable at a floor of 0.4. What makes this a Sorcerer spell rather than a Brawler one is deliberately left unstated: the critical chance no longer says it, and the answer is a design decision rather than a bound.

spell:rejuvenate.name: Rejuvenate
spell:rejuvenate.intent: The cheapest healing in the game and the reason a Sorcerer team can outlast a Brawler team. Its price sets the whole healing line: every other heal has to justify costing more than this one.
keep: The cheapest heal
Single target
spell:rejuvenate.note: Its critical chance became a live number with ADR 0033 -- the multiplier reaches a direct heal -- so the 0.17 it had been carrying as decoration is now worth 0.68 of expected healing, and it is a knob. The cheapest heal setting the price of the line is exactly the spell whose expected size should be tunable without moving the number a reader sees.

spell:meteor.name: Meteor
spell:meteor.intent: The Wizard's sweep, and the spell that says what reach costs: each enemy takes less than one of them would take from a single-target spell of the same depth, and the whole line is worth more than any of them. It opens the class whose three spells are all about reach, so it is the one that has to make the trade legible -- a sweep that hit as hard per target as a bolt would simply be a bolt that hits three.
keep: Reaches three enemies
Each of them takes less than a single-target spell of its tier deals: reach is paid for per target
The strongest thing in its tier, but by a step and not by half again
spell:meteor.note: Its bounds used to defer to Tornado -- 'these two are priced against each other or one of them is dead content' -- and Tornado is a tier deeper and disabled, so this spell was deferring its numbers to one nobody can cast while it became the ceiling of its own tier. Read per round, four damage on three targets was 12.00 against `enraged_charge`'s 8.40, 43% clear of everything; three is 9.00, a step ahead rather than a different game. The damage floor drops to 2 so a real per-target discount is reachable, and the cap to 4 so it can never hit as hard per target as `lightning_bolt` does on one. When Tornado is enabled the comparison comes back, and it is a comparison between two sweeps rather than a reason to leave this one unpriced.

spell:engulfing_flames.name: Engulfing Flames
spell:engulfing_flames.intent: The clean nuke. The catalogue holds three big single-target hits at three energy and this is the only one that costs its caster nothing -- Psycho Rush leaves the Berserker open for a round, Hateful Sacrifice takes four of the Leech's own health, and the Wizard simply casts.
keep: No caster effect: what separates it from Psycho Rush and Hateful Sacrifice is that it pays nothing
It pays for that once, in critical chance, and not twice
The Wizard's single-target answer to its own sweep
spell:engulfing_flames.note: Its old intent read 'Psycho Rush in a robe: the same cost, the same damage, the same critical chance and the same targeting', and its first keep was 'must stop being a copy of Psycho Rush'. That was settled by the **Berserker** pass, not by this spell: Psycho Rush now carries 10 damage, a chance of 0.5 and a recoil on its own caster. The claim is withdrawn. What was left was a spell paying twice for the one thing that makes it itself -- 9 damage *and* a chance of 0.33 against the other two's 10 and 0.5, for the privilege of costing nothing. Damage goes to **10**, so the discount is taken once, in the chance alone: 7.98 a round to **8.87**, between Psycho Rush's 9.13 and Hateful Sacrifice's 7.33. The `check-knobs` finding against `ice_spear` stays and is **twice an artifact**: `cast_value` has no kill term, which is what a nuke is for, and prices `ice_spear`'s slow at 2.1 a point, which is 41% of that spell's reading. Measured on content `eca50723`, after [ADR 0042](../../docs/adr/0042-a-creature-has-no-base-critical-chance.md) took the crit floor off every cast, the gap is **wider than when this note was written**, not narrower: the two win **71.2% and 44.1%** of the sides that declare them, where they read 44.4% and 49.0% before, and this one now takes 690 damage to its 653 in **77 landed casts against 127**. The spell the report calls the bar is the one losing more than it wins, which is why the way out is not this spell's bounds and is probably not the Wizard's either: it is the missing kill term.

spell:ice_spear.name: Ice Spear
spell:ice_spear.intent: Damage that also slows: a hit now and initiative off the target for a round. It is the Wizard's answer to going second and the only offensive spell that touches the timeline.
keep: Damage and slow in one cast
A rate spell, not a nuke: it wins the next round, not this one
spell:ice_spear.note: Its bounds are narrowed, not its numbers. The slow could reach 3 points over 2 rounds, which at 2.1 a point is a tempo term of 12.60 against the 4.20 it carries today -- a ceiling of **20.60**, the third largest in the catalogue, on the one weight three entries in a row have now called suspect. The duration knob went first because it contradicts the second keep above: 'it wins the next round' is one round, and a knob that can spend two is not a bound on the spell but a way out of its own identity -- the same thing `tranquilizer_dart`'s duration knob was. The amount stops at 2, which is where the content sat when these bounds were drawn. Ceiling 20.60 to **12.20**; nothing a build reads has moved. This spell was also the bar two others could not clear (`engulfing_flames` at a ceiling of 10.00, `tranquilizer_dart` at 10.00, against its 10.20), and **41% of its 10.20 was that slow**. It read 49.0% against `engulfing_flames`'s 44.4% while doing less than half the damage, so the gap the check reported was already far larger than the gap that was there. On content `eca50723`, after [ADR 0042](../../docs/adr/0042-a-creature-has-no-base-critical-chance.md) took the crit floor off every cast, that reading has **inverted rather than narrowed**: this spell wins **44.1%** of the sides that declare it against `engulfing_flames`'s **71.2%**, and the damage it was losing on it has caught up only by casting far more often -- 653 to 690, in **127 landed casts against 77**. So the check does not merely overstate a gap; it names as the bar the spell that loses more than it wins. Read that as an argument about `cast_value`, which has no kill term, and not as a reason to move these bounds: lowering a spell already at 44.1% to satisfy a number that is wrong about it fixes the report and not the game. Tune run 9 then moved it anyway, and in the shape that argument asks for rather than the one tune 8 took: the slow 2 points to **1**, the cost back 3 to **2**. On content `7e199df4` it carries **8.10**, a quarter of it the slow, and it is no longer the bar for anything -- `check-knobs` now names `soul_devourer` at 10.10 for both spells that used to be measured against this one. What the cheaper price bought is small and real: tune 8's cost of 3 had taken it to **zero** casts, and it is back at **9** landed casts of tier 3's 1589, which is `barely cast` rather than dead.

spell:summon_minions.name: Summon Minions
spell:summon_minions.intent: The only cast in the catalogue that does nothing when it lands: the minions are raised, and they gnaw at the whole enemy line over the rounds that follow. Raising them is paid in the Necromancer's own health, so the class opens on a bargain rather than on a blow -- patience bought with life. It is what both its children inherit: `crazed_specter`'s reach and `revenant_guards`' willingness to pay.
keep: Nothing lands now: every point of its damage is deferred, which is what makes it a summon and not an attack
It is paid in the summoner's own health, never in anyone else's
It reaches the whole enemy line: one minion each, not three on one
spell:summon_minions.note: Two firsts, and they are the design: no other spell defers all of its damage, and no other spell charges its caster health (ADR 0031). It used to be `EnergyGain 3` for 2, an approximation of the minions the two spells behind it spent -- and ADR 0020 named it as one of the two candidates for `EnergyRegeneration`. That nomination is declined here, with a measurement: energy was 0.2 a point then and is 0.3 since ADR 0037, so an energy spell tops out around 1.60 an activation and 2.40 today, against an attack's 6 and up either way, and `momentum` was measured cast 0 times at `explore:0.2` and 8 at `explore:0.5` after being given exactly that treatment. Two energy openers would have been two dead openers. It was then briefly `DefenseBuff 1` for two rounds on three allies, which measured fine and read as nothing: a smaller `revenant_guards`, the spell it is supposed to open rather than rehearse.

spell:revenant_guards.name: Revenant Guards
spell:revenant_guards.intent: Thundering Seal for the whole team, paid in the Necromancer's own blood: permanent defense on three allies at once, and three health off whoever raised them. It is the willingness to pay its parent names, spent on the team instead of on the enemy.
keep: Team-wide and permanent: the strongest defensive cast in the game
Priced above the single-target version or it simply replaces it -- and the price is health, not energy
The caster pays: a Necromancer never gets a cast for nothing
spell:revenant_guards.note: Its second keep was **false**. It asks to be priced above `thundering_seal` and both cost two energy, so the team-wide version simply replaced the single-target one -- 15.60 a round against 9.75, the second-largest reading in the catalogue and above a tier-3 band of 8 to 14. Legacy says why: `MinionsCost = 1`, a second currency the port dropped for this spell and for `crazed_specter` (`docs/domain/spells.md`, 'Minions'). `summon_minions` already settled what a minion costs when it charged the summoner's own health, so spending one costs the same: **4 health on the caster**, as a one-round `Bleed` (ADR 0031). 15.60 to **12.40**, inside the band, and the keep is true in the currency that matters -- `thundering_seal` costs two energy and nothing else, this costs two energy *and* four health. No energy price moved. The price is a bleed and not a `Damage` because **this spell would otherwise pay its own price down**: `Ally` targeting includes the caster (`TargetingRules`), so every cast permanently armours the summoner, and `ResolutionRules` reduces a caster `Damage` by that armour -- 3 health on the first cast, 1 on the second, 0 on the third. A bleed tick ignores defense (ADR 0019), so the toll is the same every time. `ResolutionRulesTests` pins the difference. Its critical chance is still not a knob after ADR 0033: the multiplier reaches a target's damage and direct heal, and this spell does neither -- it is the one shape the rule leaves out.

spell:crazed_specter.name: Crazed Specter
spell:crazed_specter.intent: The heaviest sweep in the game, and the Necromancer bleeds for it: against a whole team it is the single biggest swing anywhere, and three health off the caster every time it is thrown. Reach is what this class inherits from its opener; paying for it is the other half.
keep: The heaviest sweep
The minion it costs is paid in the summoner's health, the currency `summon_minions` set
It hits harder than `tornado` and pays something `tornado` does not, or the two are one spell
spell:crazed_specter.note: It was `tornado` with more damage and nothing else -- same energy, same critical chance, same Spell initiative, same three enemies, 6 against 4 -- so `check-knobs` reported it as strictly better, correctly, and the pair was one spell written twice. Its own second keep said 'its price stands in for the missing minion cost' while its price was `tornado`'s exactly, standing in for nothing. Legacy carries `MinionsCost = 1` on it, dropped at the port, and `summon_minions` already fixed what a minion costs by charging the summoner's health. So the specter costs **4 health**, as a one-round `Bleed` (ADR 0031): 15.96 a round to **13.83**, inside the band from above it, and the domination is gone because more damage now comes with a price `tornado` does not pay. The energy cost did not move -- it was never what was missing. The toll is a bleed rather than a `Damage` so that armour cannot soften it, which is what makes it a minion's due and not a wound: its sibling `revenant_guards` proved the point by armouring its own caster and paying its price down to nothing in three casts.

spell:healing_screech.name: Healing Screech
spell:healing_screech.intent: The one heal that arrives in pieces: a quarter of it now and the rest over the next two rounds, so it rewards healing before the damage lands rather than after. Regeneration exists in the taxonomy for it (ADR 0019). It is also where the Shaman's tier step lives -- 8 health against `rejuvenate`'s 4 for the same price -- and the step is entirely in the part that has to be bought early.

spell:restorative_burst.name: Restorative Burst
spell:restorative_burst.intent: Health and energy in one cast on one ally: the Shaman's tempo spell and the only way a creature other than the caster gains energy on demand -- `wait` is the only other spell that hands energy out at all, and it hands it to itself.

Single target
It trades heal for energy point for point against `restorative_gush`, whatever the weights say the trade is worth
spell:restorative_burst.note: **3.80 a round against a tier-3 band of 8 to 14, with a ceiling of 4.10** -- the worst reading in the catalogue now that `death_squad` is fixed, and its bounds cannot reach the band. Do not read them as a route to one: half the spell is 2 energy at 0.3 a point, which is 0.60, and to clear 8 on the heal alone it would need to heal 10 -- more than `restorative_gush`, the pure heal it is supposed to be a choice beside. This is `momentum`'s situation exactly, and the way out that entry names has since been tried: ADR 0037 swept the **price of energy** and moved it 0.2 to 0.3, which took this spell 3.60 to 3.80 and its ceiling 3.80 to 4.10, nowhere near the band. The heal goes 3 to **4**, the top of its box that keeps every clause above, so the trade against `restorative_gush` is 2 heal for 2 energy rather than 3 for 2: 2.80 to **3.60** at the price of the day, which fixes nothing structural and is said here so nobody reads it as a fix. And the argument is `soul_devourer`'s drain read from the other side -- giving an ally two energy does not give it 0.60 of anything, it buys it the cast it was saving for, and nothing in the scorers reads a cast bought any more than it reads a cast denied. **It has since survived a rules change that moved everything else and is still not cast.** On content `eca50723` -- base critical chance gone, every condition but Stun stacking, `player1WinShare` 0.695 to 0.475 and matches a round longer -- it is the catalogue's one `spellsNeverCast` and the only spell of 36 that does not appear in `spellOutcomes` at all. So this is the one finding of the ten that is neither an artifact of the reading nor a bound waiting to be widened: the box cannot reach the band, the arithmetic above says why, and the two ways out are both design decisions rather than numbers -- give the spell a shape the reading can price, or take it out. Nobody has taken that decision, and a tuning pass will go on reporting that it found nothing here as though it had looked in the right place.

spell:toxic_waves.intent: Bleed on a whole team: a hit now and a wound on every enemy for the rounds after. It is what makes a Shaman team win the rounds it did not act in.
keep: Team-wide bleed
What it has over `tornado` is that it keeps working, not that it costs more
spell:toxic_waves.note: Its second keep read 'costs more than Tornado because it keeps working', and it was **true until this refonte**: `tornado` cost 2 and this costs 3. The Berserker pass took `tornado` to 3 for its own reasons -- it was the second-largest reading in the catalogue and matches were ending at 6.4 rounds -- and falsified this clause on the way past, the same way it falsified `tranquilizer_dart`'s. So the clause is rewritten to what is true and was always the real point -- the lingering, not the receipt. The bleed duration knob drops from 3 rounds to 2: legacy carries `Length = 1` and so does the content, and a knob that triples a bleed across three targets took the ceiling to **26.40**, the second largest in the catalogue.
